item.title: Show HN: Agent Archive - Session Handoffs and Backups for Claude Code and Codex (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description: I often switch between Claude Code and Codex throughout the week, and between my laptop and an older machine I leave running at home. I built agent-archive to make it easier to pick up where I left off, especially when i hit usage limits. It lets you (or a coding agent) find past coding sessions and hand their conversation context to another agent. You can try local handoffs without setup, or connect your own S3/R2 bucket for automatic archiving and access from other machines. It also tracks usage across agents and gives you a full archive of your session transcripts across agents, which I've found useful to iterating and improving my AGENTS.md and lint rules. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50168300 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

item.title: Show HN: Stop Claude Code from compacting mid-task (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description: I run long sessions with Claude. For a long time I've had Claude in the middle of some difficult coding task, and then I see the auto-compact message pop up. Every time I wonder if Claude actually picks everything up correctly and nothing is lost. Claude told me 78/82 auto-compactions landed while Claude was working. For a while I couldn't do much. At first I made a skill that would make Claude explicitly save progress throughout long runs. But that didn't fix the core problem and cost more tokens as well. Now that mods came out, I fixed the actual problem. catnap tells Claude at 50% context what the context is and that it should finish what it's working on, write a handoff, and then initialize compaction itself. When Claude finishes its task, catnap compacts, and Claude can then pick up work again. The handoff replaces Claude Code's default summary, so we don't do similar work twice. If Claude for some reason doesn't compact before 60%, it gets a stricter note. And Claude Code's default auto-compact kicks in at 70% as a backstop. The 3 numbers are all settings. After I took on catnap, 0 of 129 naps came mid-task: 98 of them in benchmarks and 31 in my own sessions. The cost is the same as the default auto-compact kicking in at the same point, in tokens and dollars, on 200K and 1M context windows. Compared to the default auto-compaction that kicks in when context is nearly full, catnap used 56% fewer tokens. But lowering the default auto-compact will get you most of the way there as well. I measured memory today as well. Claude worked through tasks one message at a time while 20 instructions and facts were said in the chat, inside long chatty messages, and nowhere else. Asked right after compaction to list them from memory, no file reads: all 20 were listed with catnap and with the default compaction, in every run (15 with catnap, 5 with the default). So in my tests the memory was exactly the same, but catnap got there with a handoff 60% shorter (4.0K tokens against 10K). I was surprised that catnap is actually faster than the default option. This wasn't even one of the reasons I wanted to make this, it just happened. Since Claude writes the handoff in one go instead of the separate summary call the default makes, and the note is shorter, tasks finish sooner: measured end to end, 406 seconds instead of 464. Try it with nothing installed: npx github:LippInc/catnap It prints how often auto-compact cut in mid-task in your own logs (reads numbers only, sends nothing). Install (needs Claude Code 2.1.287 or later, where mods are on by default): claude plugin marketplace add LippInc/catnap claude plugin install catnap@lippinc Currently Claude Code only, tested on Windows and Linux. The memory test used made-up coding tasks on a 200K window. Some related tools: compact-adviser, handoff-compact, session-pilot and sub-agent-compact. What catnap adds: Claude finishes its piece first, and the numbers on where the cut lands. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50168091 Points: 1 # Comments: 0

item.title: Show HN: Jev Cards, Can you beat a vision model at a picture quiz? (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description: I built a quiz game around TypeSafe's new Jev model, which has vision capabilities. Jev looks at a picture and a question and picks an answer (or taps a place) in about a quarter of a second. I've always loved quiz games and thought this would be a fun way to see what it can do and how fast it is. I made the cards from scratch, and Jev gets exactly the picture you see. More cards will come over time. Play against Jev on your own (there's a leaderboard for each mode), or start a live match and challenge your friends, with Jev as one more player. The code is open source, so feel free to build your own game or make more cards that I can publish. Play: https://jevcards.com Code: https://github.com/Jose-Sabater/jevcards (the newest cards stay private for a while) Disclaimer: I ran Jev through both TypeSafe and Opper, and made the cards through Opper's vision models and Claude Code. I work at Opper, but you don't need anything from Opper to play Jev Cards or to run it yourself. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50167617 Points: 6 # Comments: 1

item.title: Launch HN: Respan (YC W24) - Open-source Rust AI gateway built around plugins (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description: Hey HN, this is Andy from Respan (https://www.respan.ai). We are building an open-source Rust AI gateway. It is a decoupled gateway, so everything is a plugin, including different providers, protocols (MCP, voice), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features (fallbacks, PII redaction, smart routing). Instead of packaging tons of providers and features into one gateway, Respan provides a small core and public interfaces that teams can use to assemble the AI infrastructure their application needs. That way, users can build their own features as additional plugins without having to change the gateway's core. Here's a video demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pVv2ibXiTXM There are countless LLM gateways and most of them solve a common problem: calling different providers from a single endpoint. However, adding new features can become prohibitively difficult. So developers can end up building another gateway to solve a specific problem. We've been building our gateway based on LiteLLM since 2024, and now it's providing services for thousands of orgs. Each org needs different API key settings, routes, and limits. To support that, we kept wrapping LiteLLM, adding more features to it, and at one stage, our wrapper code exceeded 100,000 lines. This January, a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection errors, and we had to roll back. We still haven't figured out the cause, but since then, we no longer upgrade LiteLLM directly and instead manually backport upstream fixes. These experiences made us realize that continuing to patch LiteLLM is not a sustainable long-term solution, and we had to redesign the gateway ourselves. While redesigning our gateway, we wanted to make it easier to add features without breaking existing ones. Inspired by Nginx, we think an AI gateway should have a really small core, only responsible for dispatching events. We believe that everything should be a plugin in our gateway, including providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini), protocols (chat, realtime voice, MCP), modalities (images, videos), and gateway features for reliability and security (smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction through example plugins). Beyond that, we want developers to be able to easily extend the gateway's capabilities by adding their own plugins, without touching the core. Adding a provider, even your own, is dead simple, because quirks are plugins too and there's nothing magical about them. A provider is a short file, Mistral's is 22 lines, and each quirk, like Groq putting token usage in its own field, gets its own test. Respan Gateway does more than let you call Claude or Gemini models from the OpenAI SDK. It handles tools, images, and reasoning protocols automatically: an application based on the OpenAI Realtime API can also use Gemini Live through the gateway, though not every feature translates. A simple chat app can use MCP tools configured in the gateway, without implementing MCP itself. We also parse requests into a shared structure. When the client and provider use the same API, we preserve provider-specific fields in their native format, even if our shared structure doesn't have a field for them. That way, the gateway can write them back instead of dropping them. Here's how it works: An adapter hands each HTTP or WebSocket connection to the first client format that recognizes it. The format exposes the request as a two-way stream of typed input and output events. The core runs plugins in registration order, allowing them to choose a provider, filter or wrap either stream, make additional calls, return a response, or refuse the request. A provider format then opens the upstream connection. If the client and provider use the same format and no plugin changes the payload, the original bytes and protocol-specific fields can pass through unchanged. When formats differ, they translate through shared types for messages, tool calls, results, streams, and usage. This stream model can represent both one-shot HTTP requests and long-lived bidirectional sessions. The gateway is open source at https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway under the MIT or Apache-2.0 license. You don't need to use Respan's hosted platform and can run it directly on your local machine. Build it from source, add your provider keys, and swap the base URL in a supported client. You can keep using the API your client already speaks. It's still pre-alpha. We make money from our hosted platform (https://www.respan.ai/pricing), which runs the gateway for you with native observability and evals, along with unified billing. If you're building routing, tools, filtering, observability, or security for agents, we'd love to see it as a plugin. PLUGINS.md in the repo explains how to write one and links to the plugins we've created so far. Turning that into an ecosystem is basically our roadmap, and we welcome you to contribute your own plugins. We'd love to answer any questions and hear your feedback! https://github.com/respanai/respan-gateway Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50167583 Points: 11 # Comments: 1

item.title: Show HN: VoidAccess - open-source dark web OSINT, from query to a graph (Source: hnrss.org | Category: Hacker News)
item.description: Hi HN! Im Katriel, and im a Security Researcher/Enthusiast and in the wave of AI, i wanted to build that next gen of security tooling that surpasses the current tools, and even the paid industries with an open source engine. I built MailAccess as well, which is going to be the best damn email osint tool out there, in another year. But just before building MailAccess i built VoidAccess, because i was delving a lot into DarkINT and the content inside the dark web is too difficult to navigate through for a human, so i automated that pipeline, made sure the noise was removed, and anything NSFW was filtered out, to give the analyst an overview of what is present in the dark web, without having to actually go through it manually. Very simple to run, you just run a few commands to install, and a couple to investigate. Then the engine takes over, and stops onyl when the job is done(or at a particular time limit, if set by the user). Do check it out, if that is something that interests you. Thanks to the community for giving it the love it has got till now. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50167286 Points: 74 # Comments: 6
